title: Bir Tawil, the land no country claims
hook: A patch of desert that neither of its neighbours wants to claim.
peek: Between Egypt and Sudan lies Bir Tawil, about 2,000 square kilometres of desert that neither country claims. It is not unwanted for its own sake: claiming it would weaken each side's case for a larger, more valuable area nearby.
lede: Bir Tawil is a trapezoid of dry, rocky land on the border between Egypt and Sudan, roughly 2,000 square kilometres in size. It has no permanent population and no government. It is one of the very few pieces of land on Earth that no state claims. The reason lies in two different lines drawn on the map more than a century ago.

bullets.text: A border set in 1899 follows the 22nd parallel. An administrative line drawn in 1902 bends away from it in two places. Egypt favours the 1899 line, and Sudan the 1902 line.

Each line hands one area to each country. The other area, the Halaib Triangle on the Red Sea coast, is roughly ten times larger. Claiming Bir Tawil would mean accepting the line that gives Halaib away, so neither side does.

Land that no state claims is called terra nullius. Bir Tawil is often cited as the clearest example on land today, since the larger unclaimed part of Antarctica sits under a treaty that sets claims aside.
Several people have travelled there, planted flags and announced new countries. None of these claims has been recognised by any government, and they have no legal standing.
